title: Strategies to increase clinician-reviewed symptom measurement in outpatient depression care: a systematic review
abstract: Objective: to compare strategies that increase completed and clinician-reviewed symptom measures in outpatient depression care, and whether the increases last after support ends. Methods: systematic review with uptake definitions coded against a core definition, structured synthesis and meta-analysis where at least three studies are comparable. Results will follow screening.
introduction: Measurement-based care is widely recommended for depression, but uptake is low and defined in at least eleven ways. Effects of prompts and feedback often fade after support ends, and outcome benefits depend on clinicians acting on the scores.
methods: The librarian searches four databases and two trial registers. Two reviewers screen and extract independently and code each study's uptake definition against the core definition of a completed measure reviewed by the clinician at the same visit. Studies are grouped by the step of the measurement chain they act on; pooling uses random effects only within comparable groups.
results: Screening has not started. The report will give uptake by strategy type, persistence after support ends, and response or remission where reported.
discussion: To be written against the service's pending choice between an electronic prompt and clinician training with feedback. The discussion will weigh durability as heavily as the initial gain.
limitations: English and French only; heterogeneous definitions; possibly a single reviewer if the second reviewer is not released.
